title: Senior's toolkit: finding injection
summary: sqlmap to prove an injection (on systems you may test), Semgrep and CodeQL to find concatenated queries and shells in code, EF Core's EF1002 and the .NET CA rules as build errors, and ToQueryString to see the SQL.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding injection
steps.body: Injection is found two ways: from the outside by sending payloads, and from the inside by tracing user input (a source) to a query or a shell (a sink). Seniors use both, and make the build refuse the patterns that cause it.

toolkit.what: Detect and exploit SQL injection automatically: boolean, error, UNION, stacked and time-based techniques, then dump tables. Only against systems you are authorised to test: it sends thousands of requests.
flags: the target, with a normal value
read a table once injection is confirmed

toolkit.what: Pattern-based static analysis that reads like code: finds string-built SQL, Process.Start with a shell, Html.Raw on input. Fast enough for every pull request; write your own rules for your codebase's helpers.
flags: the community C# rules (also p/owasp-top-ten, p/secrets)
exit 1 on findings, to fail CI

toolkit.what: Data-flow (taint) analysis: follows a value from an HTTP parameter through method calls to a sink such as ExecuteSqlRaw or Process.Start. Slower than Semgrep, finds what pattern matching misses. GitHub code scanning runs it for you.
flags: build the code into a CodeQL database
toolkit.example:
codeql database create db --language=csharp --command='dotnet build'
codeql database analyze db codeql/csharp-queries:codeql-suites/csharp-security-extended.qls --format=sarif-latest --output=codeql.sarif

toolkit.what: Make the compiler refuse injection-prone code: EF1002 (interpolated string in FromSqlRaw/ExecuteSqlRaw), CA2100 (SQL text from a non-constant), CA3001-CA3012 (taint rules: SQL, process, file path, XSS; enable them first, they are off by default).
flags: EF Core analyzer, on by default
review SQL queries for security vulnerabilities
the .editorconfig way to turn one on

toolkit.what: Print the SQL EF Core will send, with its parameters declared. The quickest proof in review that a value became a parameter (@p0, @__q_0) and not text.
flags: the SQL and DECLARE lines for the parameters
toolkit.example:
var pattern = "%" + q + "%";
Console.WriteLine(db.Products.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Products WHERE Name LIKE {pattern}").ToQueryString());

steps.prompt: Match each tool to how it finds injection.
pairs: sends payloads to a running app
matches code patterns, fast, on every PR
follows tainted data from source to sink
a compiler warning for interpolated FromSqlRaw
shows the SQL and its parameters

steps.prompt: Test only the `q` parameter of the lab's search, without questions, and read the users table.

Semgrep reports no SQL injection, but a pentest finds one: the query is built in `ReportBuilder.AddFilter(string column, string value)`, three calls away from the controller. Which tool is designed for exactly this?
options: CodeQL (taint tracking): it follows the request value through the calls to the sink
steps.explain: Pattern matching sees one place at a time; data-flow analysis follows values across methods. In practice teams run both: Semgrep for speed and custom rules, CodeQL for depth.
